cells.tense: The care is steady and it runs on its own supply, not on the other person's response.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're tending, and say out loud where it's finished. Then let that part be finished. Today, in your own words.
cells.core:
What you're looking after is actually getting stronger. You can hold something steady without clamping down on it, and you can wait through the slow part without calling the slow part a failure. That's not patience as a virtue — it's patience as a skill, and it's working.

It works because you let things be done. When something reaches the end of what you can give it, you hand it off, or you let it stand, and you don't keep poking it to prove you're still needed. A good year here looks like things you started that no longer need you. What keeps it: you still have to notice the moment it's done, and that moment is quieter than the urge to keep going.
cells.sheetLine: Let the finished thing be finished, and don't take it back up.
cells.place: the table where the finished work gets set down

cells.tense: You are bracing for a version of this that hasn't arrived, and you're writing the ending before anyone else gets to.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're managing closely. For one day, do nothing to it — no check, no fix, no nudge — and write down what you wanted to do.
cells.core:
Your care has gone past what the thing needs. You're holding the shape of what's coming before it's had a chance to form, steering it away from an outcome you can picture and can't stand. What you give is real. The extra is the grip.

When this is steady, you hold something loosely and it still turns out. You're needed for the conditions, not for every move. In this stretch the person is inside the work, and they can feel you in there. Letting one day go unfixed won't hurt them. It also won't tell you what they need — you'll only find that out by not deciding it first.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding it so tight there's no room left for it to grow.
cells.place: the table where the finished work gets set down

cells.tense: You stopped tending at a door you're still standing in front of, and the room is behind you now.
cells.ask: Do one small piece of care for something of yours — a plant, a page, a meal — and let it be enough for the day.
cells.core:
Nothing's growing because nothing's being fed. The care is still there under the surface, but it's pointed inward at staying upright, and staying upright doesn't produce anything. What looks like not needing anyone is mostly the arms staying folded.

The version of this that works doesn't start with a big opening up. It starts with something small you actually want to keep alive, and giving it a little attention without asking it to become anything yet. That's not a mood you wait to find. It's a thing you do, the same size tomorrow, and it builds something you can point at.
cells.sheetLine: You folded your arms to stay steady, and nothing gets fed that way.
cells.place: the table where the finished work gets set down

cells.tense: You are already doing the tending, in a room you keep describing as just how things are.
cells.ask: Find one thing you're carrying that nobody handed you. Say plainly whose it is, then hand it back or put it down, today.
cells.core:
People come to you with their weight and you take it, and you talk about it like it just happens. The care runs the whole time — it shapes your week, your mood, what you cancel — and you'd say you're being practical about it. The doing is real. The owning of it isn't there.

When this is steady, you choose what you pick up, and you can set down what isn't yours without it being a betrayal. Nothing about being the one people lean on is wrong. What's off is that it happened without a decision, and the cost lands on you quietly. One small hand-back won't end anything. It'll just show you where the line is.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying a load you didn't agree to, and calling it normal.
cells.place: the table where the finished work gets set down

attempts.check: The record never says the person has been made into a caretaker by anyone else — only that others experience them that way, which could equally be their own appetite for being needed. The reader could reasonably say 'no one assigned me this, I keep volunteering,' and that would still fit every bit of the map. The ask survives being wrong either way: setting down one thing is useful whoever picked it up. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you never chose this' — it hands them an excuse instead of a claim, so I'm writing the seat record of what they do rather than a story of how they got there.
